How New Jersey sets property tax

Value drives the tax, and local budgets turn that value into a bill. Each parcel is measured against true value, meaning the price a willing buyer and a willing seller would agree on in an open sale, fixed on one statutory snapshot date in the autumn before the tax year. All 21 counties assess at the full 100 percent of that value.

Equalization compares the 566 taxing districts so that county government and shared school costs are split fairly between towns. A municipality finds its general rate by dividing the amount its budget must raise by the combined assessed value of everything taxable inside its borders. Your bill is that rate times your assessment, and the State itself receives none of the money.

Because the amount comes out of county, municipal and school budgets, you cannot contest the tax as such. You can only contest the assessment underneath it.

Due dates and penalties

Four payments fall due across the year: Feb. 1, May 1, Aug. 1 and Nov. 1. A missed installment starts accruing interest. Unpaid tax on real estate is a continuous lien, so the debt follows the house into any sale.

A late balance may be charged up to 8 percent annually on its first $1,500 and up to 18 percent on whatever exceeds that figure. When a town's overdue total tops $10,000 at fiscal year end, it may add a further penalty of up to 6 percent. Municipalities collect these amounts, so call the tax collector for a dated payoff instead of estimating from a bill.

How to appeal your assessment

The route runs through your County Board of Taxation, and the calendar is strict. The filing cutoff is April 1 each year, or 45 days after assessment notices are mailed in bulk. A town that has just finished a revaluation or reassessment moves the cutoff to May 1. Three counties, Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth, run a different assessment calendar, and their cutoff is January 15.

You carry the burden of proof, and the board weighs true market value against the taxable assessment. Evidence should predate the October 1 assessment date. A strong petition usually includes:

  • three to five sales of similar homes, attached when you file
  • photographs of your home and of each comparable
  • copies of those comparables delivered to both the assessor and the board a week or more before the hearing
  • an income statement, if the property is commercial

Hearings generally take place within three months of the filing cutoff, and the board must decide within that same window. Adjournments are rarely granted. If you skip the hearing, the case can end for lack of prosecution, and that closes the door to the Tax Court. The assessments of neighboring properties do not count as proof, so lean on actual sales.

The common level range

To show an assessment is excessive or discriminatory, you must prove it misses the True Market Value Standard or the Common Level Range Standard. The range extends 15 percent above and below the Director's Ratio, the average assessed-to-true-value percentage the State certifies for each taxing district.

If your property's ratio lands above the range, the board resets taxable value by multiplying true value by the district's average ratio. A win also brings the Freeze Act into play: the new figure stays put for that year and the following two, unless a revaluation or an added assessment intervenes or you appeal again.

Relief programs for homeowners

ANCHOR is the largest, and it pays by income band. Using 2025 income, homeowners at or below $150,000 get $1,500, while those between $150,001 and $250,000 get $1,000. Renters receive $450, or $700 if they were 65 or older by the end of 2025. Checks go out on a rolling schedule beginning September 15, typically within 90 days of the application. All relief combined cannot exceed the property tax actually paid on the main home.

Senior Freeze repays seniors and disabled residents for tax increases on their main home, measured from a base year, and the Stay NJ credit rides on the same combined form. Senior citizen, disabled person and veteran deductions also count toward the cap. Check the Division of Taxation's relief page when a new application round opens.

Does the owner lose the house at a tax sale?

No, not at the auction. The sale puts a lien up for bid, and the title stays with the owner. Every municipality with delinquent taxes or charges must hold at least one sale yearly. Bidders compete by lowering the interest rate they will accept, starting from 18 percent. When bids reach one percent, they switch to offering a premium.

You can redeem the certificate by paying the amount owed plus a redemption penalty of 2, 4 or 6 percent, set by the certificate's size. Foreclosure is possible only after two years: the certificate holder may then sue in Superior Court, and a successful suit moves the deed to the holder. Learn your town's sale schedule from the collector well ahead of time.

Selling with taxes owed

Start with the tax collector. Request a written payoff that lists current installments, interest and any other municipal charges, and ask whether a tax sale is on the calendar. Hand that figure to the title agent so the amount is settled out of the sale. Before you agree to a closing date, line up these items:

  • the payoff letter, dated close to the settlement day
  • the date of the next tax sale, if the property is delinquent
  • proof of any ANCHOR, Senior Freeze or deduction benefit already received
  • the status of any open assessment appeal, which may produce a refund or a changed bill

At closing, the title agent pays the collector from your proceeds and the lien comes off the house. A payoff dated close to settlement matters because interest keeps running until the day the money arrives. A cash sale skips the buyer's mortgage underwriting, so the closing date is easier to fix once you know the payoff and any sale date.

Frequently asked questions

Can I appeal the tax bill itself in New Jersey?

No. Only the assessment can be contested. The amount owed comes from local budgets, so the petition goes to the county board, aimed at the value, before the cutoff that applies where you live.

When must a New Jersey assessment petition be filed?

By April 1 in most places, or within 45 days of the bulk mailing of notices. Revaluation towns use May 1. Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth Counties use January 15.

What does ANCHOR pay a New Jersey homeowner?

It pays $1,500 to homeowners with 2025 income of $150,000 or less and $1,000 to those earning $150,001 to $250,000. Above that, a homeowner does not qualify.

How much interest builds on a late payment?

Up to 8 percent on the first $1,500 and up to 18 percent on the rest. A town may also add up to 6 percent when overdue taxes pass $10,000 at fiscal year end.

Can New Jersey take a home over delinquent taxes?

Not directly. The town auctions a lien certificate, and the holder cannot begin a Superior Court foreclosure until two years pass. Paying the certificate off, with the added penalty, ends the process.

Does New Jersey have a homestead exemption?

People searching for a New Jersey homestead exemption usually end up at the state's property tax relief programs. The Division of Taxation runs three of them for homeowners: Senior Freeze (Property Tax Reimbursement), ANCHOR and Stay NJ. All three are filed on one combined application, the PAS-1. Municipalities add their own deductions on top.

These programs pay benefits to qualifying owners. They are tied to a principal residence and to income, and eligibility rules, income limits and benefit amounts depend on appropriation in the State Budget, so they can shift from year to year. Check the Division's relief page for the current filing season, and keep your most recent benefit statement and property tax bill handy when you apply.

Which relief program fits which homeowner

The three programs overlap, and the Division decides which benefits an applicant gets. Here is how they compare for the 2025 application year.

Property tax relief programs, 2025 application year
ProgramWho qualifiesIncome limit
ANCHORHomeowners who owned and occupied the home on October 1, 2025, and renters$250,000 for homeowners, $150,000 for renters
Senior FreezeAge 65 or older, or receiving Social Security or Railroad Retirement disability, and owned and lived in the home since December 31, 2022 or earlier$172,475 for 2025
Stay NJHomeowners 65 or older who owned and lived in the home all 12 months of 2025$200,000 or less

A homeowner under 65 who does not receive Social Security disability can qualify only for ANCHOR. A homeowner who is 65 or older may qualify for all three.

How much Stay NJ pays

The maximum depends on income. For the 2027 payments covering the 2025 tax year, it is $6,500 at income up to $100,000, $5,000 above that through $150,000, and $4,000 above that through $200,000. Over $200,000 the benefit is zero.

Payments arrive in installments, and the 2025 benefit is paid in February and May of 2027. Each applicant gets a benefit statement listing the Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ amounts.

One cap applies to all three programs: total relief cannot exceed the property taxes paid on the principal residence for the qualifying year. Relief payments are not taxable income for New Jersey state taxes.

Property and ownership rules

The home must be your principal residence, meaning the place you live most of the time and where you vote or get mail. For owners it is the property on the deed or tax records. A vacation home, a second home or a rental property does not qualify.

  • Senior Freeze: not available on property with more than four units, or with four units or fewer that contains more than one commercial unit, and not available if you make P.I.L.O.T. payments instead of property tax.
  • Stay NJ: mobile homeowners and renters are excluded, a co-owned home is calculated on your ownership percentage, and a duplex is calculated on the share of the property you occupy.
  • Trusts and life estates: a trust beneficiary, or someone with a life estate or a 99-year lease, can qualify and must send the trust, deed or lease document.

Keep the deed or tax record that names you as owner, since that is what proves the home is your principal residence if a question comes up.

Condominium owners and resident co-op shareholders who pay property tax on their unit count as homeowners.

Local property tax deductions

Municipalities handle several deductions and exemptions directly: a $250 deduction for senior citizens and disabled persons, a $250 deduction for military service, and a 100 percent exemption for service-connected disability.

The senior and disabled deduction has its own tests. The owner must be 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, or an unmarried surviving spouse age 55 or older of such a person. The owner must have lived in New Jersey for a year as of October 1 before the deduction year, owned and lived in the dwelling on that date, and kept income to $10,000 or less with certain exclusions such as Social Security. Form PTD is filed with the municipal assessor or collector, followed by a yearly income statement.

For the military-service programs and the exact forms, call the local tax assessor. These deductions come through the town, not the state application.

What happens to relief benefits if you sell or move

A homeowner who moved during the year is still eligible for ANCHOR, but the benefit follows the qualifying property owned and occupied on October 1. A divorced or separated applicant follows the same test: whoever owned and occupied the home on October 1 may apply.

The closing side works like this. When a benefit check is processed after a move has been properly shown on the application, the money goes to the seller. If the move is not shown, the seller needs to take credit for the benefit at closing, and if the seller, an attorney or the closing agent misses it, the credit lands on the new owners' taxes. That guidance was written for the Homestead Benefit, the earlier program, so ask the title company how current benefits are being handled for your closing.

Senior Freeze recipients who buy another New Jersey home must re-establish eligibility for the new property. A seller who received a reimbursement the year before moving waits two years for a new base year instead of the standard three, then files Form PTR-1-C.

Other tax breaks when selling a New Jersey home

Sales tax is not due on a home sale, and the seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee. Every seller furnishes a GIT/REP form to record the deed, and New Jersey residents use GIT/REP-3 to avoid an estimated income tax payment at closing.

A seller who qualifies for the federal principal residence exclusion can exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, after owning and living in the home two of the last five years. Nonresident sellers face an estimated payment of 2 percent of the sale price or 8.97 percent of net gain unless an exemption applies.

The transfer fee is figured per $500 of consideration, with rates that step up as the price rises and an extra Graduated Percent Fee on residential sales above $1,000,000. Ask your closing attorney for the exact fee and for which GIT/REP form you should sign, and gather your benefit statements so the title company can sort out any credit due at closing.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a homestead exemption that lowers my assessed value?

No single program works that way. New Jersey offers ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ as payments through the state, plus local deductions such as the $250 senior and disabled deduction handled by your municipality.

Who qualifies for ANCHOR as a homeowner?

A New Jersey resident who owned and lived in the home on October 1, 2025, with gross income up to $250,000. Renters qualify with income up to $150,000. The home must be the principal residence.

Can I get Stay NJ if I am under 65?

No. You or your spouse must have been 65 or older in 2025, and receiving Social Security disability does not change that. Mobile homeowners and renters are also excluded.

What if I sold my house after filing the relief application?

The benefit follows the home you owned and occupied on October 1. Show the move on the application, or take credit at closing, so the benefit does not pass to the new owners.

Do relief payments count as taxable income in New Jersey?

No. Relief payments are not taxable income for New Jersey state taxes. Each applicant's total benefits also cannot exceed the property taxes paid on the home.

Does New Jersey still have an estate tax?

No. The state estate tax stopped applying to anyone who died on or after January 1, 2018, so those estates file no estate tax return. The separate inheritance tax is still in force, and heirs of a New Jersey house are far more likely to run into it.

Old paperwork still circulates, which is why the history matters. For deaths after 2001 and before 2017, a return was required when the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts passed $675,000. For deaths during 2017, a taxable estate over $2 million triggered it, at rates from 0 to 16 percent. Only an estate from those earlier years has to deal with it now.

Who pays inheritance tax on a house

The heirs pay, and the amount depends on how they were related to the person who died. Heirs are sorted into classes and each class has its own rate. A Class A heir owes nothing.

Inheritance tax by beneficiary class
ClassWho is in itTax on what they receive
ASpouse, civil union or domestic partner, child, grandchild, parent, grandparent, stepchild, mutually acknowledged childNo tax
CBrother or sister, spouse of a child, civil union partner of a childFirst $25,000 free; 11% on the next $1,075,000; 13% on the next $300,000; 14% on the next $300,000; 16% above $1,700,000
DAnyone not in Class A, C or E, such as a friend, niece or nephew15% on the first $700,000; 16% above that
EQualified charities, religious, educational and medical institutions, the State and its subdivisionsExempt

A house left to a spouse, child or grandchild carries no inheritance tax. A house left to a sibling, a friend or a niece gets no such shelter, and the heir should plan for the bill before listing it, ideally with the executor.

The inheritance tax return deadline

Eight months from the date of death is the cutoff for both the return and the payment. An executor, administrator or heir at law files when a return is required. Unpaid tax collects interest at 10 percent a year after that date.

  • An extension never excuses late payment. Form IT-EXT stretches only the filing date.
  • Inheritance and estate tax returns cannot be filed electronically, so everything goes in on paper.
  • Form IT-R is the resident decedent return, and form IT-NR is the nonresident return.
  • For a resident who died on or after January 1, 2018, the Division's flowchart shows which return or waiver to use.

A house can sit unsold well past eight months, and interest runs the whole time. An heir who expects to owe tax should arrange payment before closing.

Getting the state waiver so the house can sell

You ask the Division of Taxation for a real property tax waiver, which releases the State's lien on the house. When the estate of a resident decedent has only Class A beneficiaries and owes no tax, form L-9 does the job. Start early, because the Division sends back any form that is incomplete or missing attachments.

Form L-9 must be notarized and signed by the executor, the administrator or a joint tenant. Attach each of these papers:

  • The will, any codicils and writings, and any trust agreement.
  • A copy of the deed to the property.
  • The letters testamentary or letters of administration.
  • The death certificate.

L-9 is off the table if any asset worth $500 or more passes to someone outside Class A, if a mutually acknowledged child is claimed, or if inheritance tax is due. A trust created by the will can lead the Division to ask for a full return. Do not file with the county clerk. Mail it to the Transfer Inheritance Tax unit at P.O. Box 249, Trenton, NJ 08695-0249. The branch answers questions at (609) 292-5033.

A surviving spouse who held the house as tenants by the entirety needs no waiver, and none is issued. Bank and brokerage accounts use a different form, the self-executing waiver IT-L-8, filed with each financial institution.

Transfer fee when an executor sells

The answer depends on whose name goes on the deed. When the executor conveys to a devisee or heir named under the will or the intestacy rules, the transfer is exempt. When the executor sells to an outside buyer, the fee is due, and the personal reduction for seniors and disabled persons is not available to an estate.

A will that tells the executor to sell and divide the cash is read as a bequest of money rather than a devise of real estate, so the sale is taxable. The estate files one GIT/REP form, which several executors can sign together. Our closing costs page covers the fee schedule.

Income tax on selling an inherited house

Inheritance tax is only one layer. A house sold after the owner's death can also produce a capital gain, measured from the heir's basis. IRS Publication 551 covers basis for inherited property, and holding periods have exceptions for property acquired from a decedent. Ask the estate's tax preparer which valuation rules fit your sale.

The federal home sale exclusion, worth up to $250,000 for one filer or $500,000 on a joint return, requires two years of use as a main home within the last five. An heir who never lived in the house usually does not meet that test. A loss on personal use property such as a home cannot be deducted.

What an heir should gather first

Collect the papers the Division wants before anything else, since the same set supports the waiver request and the later sale. If the class of an heir or the status of a trust is unclear, call the Inheritance and Estate Tax Branch at (609) 292-5033.

  • Order certified death certificates and locate the will and any trust agreement.
  • Get the executor's or administrator's certificate, meaning the letters testamentary or letters of administration.
  • Find the recorded deed and note how title was held. A surviving spouse on a tenancy by the entirety needs no waiver.
  • List every heir and the relationship to the decedent, so each can be placed in a class.
  • Mark the eight month date on a calendar, since interest accrues from that point on unpaid tax.

Heirs who plan to sell should ask early whether a waiver or a full return applies. A call to the branch can settle questions about trusts or unusual beneficiaries before a buyer is under contract. A cash buyer who accepts the house as is can shorten repairs and financing, but the waiver still controls when you can close.

Frequently asked questions

Does a recent death trigger New Jersey estate tax?

No. The state stopped imposing it for deaths from January 1, 2018 forward, so no estate tax return is needed.

Do I owe tax on a house my parent left me?

No. A child sits in Class A, and Class A heirs owe no New Jersey inheritance tax.

What do a sibling and a friend pay on an inherited house?

A sibling is Class C and pays 11 to 16 percent after the first $25,000. A friend is Class D and pays 15 percent on the first $700,000 and 16 percent above.

What is the filing window for an inheritance tax return?

Eight months after the date of death. Unpaid tax then accrues 10 percent interest per year. Payment cannot be extended, although the filing date can be.

Which form releases the state lien so the house can sell?

Form L-9, for a resident decedent whose beneficiaries are all Class A and who owes no tax. Other situations need a full inheritance tax return, which leads to the waiver.

Who pays the realty transfer fee

The seller pays it. The Realty Transfer Fee (RTF) is a state charge that the seller owes when a deed is recorded, and the supplemental percent fee lands on the seller too. Any conveyance of title to New Jersey real property is covered unless the deed or the transfer matches a listed exemption.

The amount is figured on the consideration written in the deed. In some cases the Division of Taxation instead takes the assessed value of the property and divides it by the Director's Ratio for the municipality. That ratio comes from the certification of the Table of Equalized Valuations, and filers use the prior year's certification for a deed dated in a given year.

Anyone claiming a full or partial exemption must file Form RTF-1, the Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller, with the deed. For a sheriff's sale, the applicant also files Form RTF-8, which lists other mortgagees and liens. RTF-8 is not an exemption.

Standard transfer fee rates

Brackets of $500 drive the math, and the price decides which ladder you climb. Totals of $350,000 or less use the lower ladder below.

Standard seller rates when total consideration is $350,000 or less
Consideration bracketRate per $500
$0 to $150,000$2.00
$150,000 to $200,000$3.35
$200,000 to $350,000$3.90

Once the total passes $350,000, a higher ladder applies. Its first slice, up to $150,000, runs $2.90 for each $500. The slice up to $200,000 runs $4.25 and the slice up to $550,000 runs $4.80. Beyond that you pay $5.30 up to $850,000, then $5.80 up to $1,000,000, then $6.05 on whatever remains.

The exact figure shows up on your settlement statement.

The extra percent fee on sales over $1 million

The Graduated Percent Fee, often called the mansion tax, applies when the consideration is more than $1,000,000. It is charged on the total price, and the percentage climbs with the bracket. The seller is statutorily responsible for it along with the RTF.

The percentage steps up with the price. A price over $1 million and up to $2 million draws 1 percent. Over $2 million and up to $2.5 million it is 2 percent, and over $2.5 million and up to $3 million it is 2.5 percent. Above $3 million and up to $3.5 million the fee is 3 percent, and anything over $3.5 million pays 3.5 percent.

The fee covers deeds for Class 2 residential property, Class 3A farms that contain a building suited for residential use, Class 4A commercial property other than industrial or apartment, and Class 4C cooperative units. Exemptions are claimed on Form RTF-1EE, which goes with every deed over $1 million and every commercial transfer.

Deeds exempt from the fee

Some deeds owe no RTF at all. The exemptions are read narrowly, so a transfer missing from the list pays the fee even when the reason behind it seems sympathetic. Exempt deeds include:

  • any deed with consideration under $100
  • a deed between husband and wife, or between parent and child
  • an executor's or administrator's deed to a devisee or heir that distributes the estate under the will or the intestacy laws
  • a deed filed within three months after a divorce decree ends the marriage of grantor and grantee
  • a deed that gives or releases security for a debt, or that confirms or corrects a deed already recorded
  • deeds on partition, on a sale for delinquent taxes, or from a receiver, bankruptcy trustee or assignee for creditors

Family sales, estates and trusts

Family cases produce most of the questions. A sale from parents to their daughter and son-in-law is exempt as parent to child. A father selling to his daughter and her live-in boyfriend gets an exemption on half of the price, and the other half is taxed. A legally adopted child counts as a child, but a stepchild does not unless the stepparent adopted him or her.

An executor who sells to an heir named in the will, or an heir under the intestacy rules, is exempt. A sale to anyone else is not. If a will tells the executor to sell and divide the money, the bequest is treated as a gift of money, so that sale pays the fee. Placing a house in trust for children is also taxable because the grantor gives up the benefits of ownership.

A divorce settlement that is simply folded into a judgment does not qualify as specific performance of a final judgment. The deed has to follow the decree closely, within the 90-day window, to use the divorce exemption. Attorney-prepared deeds in quitclaim form that move a freehold interest are treated as taxable transfers.

Reduced rates for seniors and disabled sellers

Lower partial rates are open to sellers who are 62 or older, to blind or disabled sellers, and to low and moderate income housing transfers. On a total of $350,000 or less, the reduced rate is $0.50 per $500 through $150,000, then $1.25 per $500 between $150,000 and $350,000.

On a total above $350,000, the reduced rates start at $1.40 per $500 for the first $150,000 and climb to $3.40 per $500 above $1,000,000. You claim the rate on a notarized Form RTF-1 recorded with the deed.

The rate belongs to the seller personally. An estate, a trust or a company cannot use it, and a senior who moves a house into a trust gives it up. On a farm sale, only the share of the price tied to the residence and the land needed to enjoy it qualifies, usually the Class 3A portion.

Where the fee is paid, and what if the county is wrong

Payment goes to the county recording officer at the counter. The land's own county is the only valid place to file. A deed that lands in a different county must be filed again in the right one, with a State refund request on Form RTF-3, and the county portion has to be reclaimed from the wrong county's recording office.

Ask the county clerk for the current recording charges, because those are county fees and sit on top of the state fee. Find the RTF line on the seller's closing statement and ask whoever runs your closing how it will reach the recording officer.

What to gather before closing

A few steps keep the fee from surprising you at the table.

  • Settle early whether an exemption or reduced rate fits, and tell the closing agent so a notarized Form RTF-1 goes to the recording office with the deed.
  • On a price above $1,000,000, expect Form RTF-1EE to travel with the deed.
  • Confirm the county where the property sits, because recording happens there.
  • Find the RTF line on the seller's closing statement and check that the bracket matches the price.

The fee comes out of the seller's proceeds at closing. A cash buyer does not change who owes it, but a quicker closing means the fee is settled sooner.

Frequently asked questions

Is the realty transfer fee paid by the buyer or the seller?

The seller pays it. The RTF is imposed on the seller for recording the deed, and the Graduated Percent Fee falls on the seller too.

Does the fee change with the sale price?

Yes. It is charged per $500 of consideration in brackets, with one schedule for prices of $350,000 or less and a steeper one above that. Sales over $1,000,000 also carry the percent fee.

Is a sale between a parent and a child exempt?

Yes, a deed between parent and child is exempt, and that includes a legally adopted child. A stepchild relationship does not qualify unless the stepparent adopted the child.

Does the senior citizen rate work if my house is in a trust?

No. The reduced rate is a personal exemption and a trust cannot use it. A senior who deeds the house to a trust and later sells through it pays the standard rates.

What form do I file to claim an exemption?

File Form RTF-1, the Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller, with the deed. It must be notarized for a partial exemption. Deeds priced above $1,000,000 also carry Form RTF-1EE for the percent fee.

Is gain on a New Jersey house sale taxable?

Yes, and it helps to know early. New Jersey counts gain on a house as income and figures it the federal way, so whatever is taxable on your federal return is taxable here too. The gain goes on the same state return as your other income, for the year of the sale.

Gain is the amount realized minus your adjusted basis, and basis starts with what you paid. If you inherited the house, IRS Publication 551 has the basis rules. A loss on a home you lived in is not deductible.

The state's top bracket matters for large gains. The Gross Income Tax rate is 10.75 percent on income above $1 million, beginning with tax year 2020, and one big sale can push a seller into it for that year.

Excluding the gain on your main home

Owners of a main home can shelter $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, once they pass the tests below. New Jersey follows the federal exclusion, and it applies whether you stay in the state or move away.

  • Ownership: you held title for at least two of the five years ending on the closing date.
  • Use: you lived in it as your main home for at least two years inside that same window.
  • Other homes: you did not exclude gain from a different home in the two years before this sale.
  • A joint-filing couple reaches $500,000 only if both spouses pass the use test. If just one qualifies, the limit is $250,000.

If you miss the two-year mark because of a job change, a health problem or another unforeseen event, you may claim a reduced exclusion. You may also get a Form 1099-S and have to report the sale to the IRS even when the whole gain is excluded (IRS Topic 701). Rental properties, second homes and vacation homes do not count as a principal residence.

Gain above the exclusion

Anything over the exclusion is a capital gain, and the federal rate depends on how long you owned the house. Held a year or less, the profit is short-term and taxed as ordinary income. Held longer, the profit is long-term and earns the lower rates of 0, 15 or 20 percent, depending on taxable income (IRS Topic 409).

Two extras can apply to sellers of residential property: a 25 percent ceiling on unrecaptured section 1250 gain, and the net investment income tax for people with significant investment income. Federal reporting goes on Form 8949 and Schedule D.

New Jersey adds its own filing steps. Residents report the gain on Schedule B of the NJ-1040 as Net Gains or Income From Disposition of Property. Nonresidents use Part I of the NJ-1040-NR. If the sale produced a loss, the state form takes a zero on that line.

Do you owe New Jersey tax at the closing table?

Only a nonresident seller pays at closing, although every seller hands in a GIT/REP form so the deed can be recorded. A seller who keeps a New Jersey residence files form GIT/REP-3, which exempts the estimated payment. Tax on any gain is then settled on the NJ-1040 the following filing season.

A New Jersey resident who sells and moves out of state counts as a nonresident for this sale. The estimated payment is 2 percent of the consideration or 8.97 percent of the net gain, sent before or at closing, and a seller's assurance on GIT/REP-3 can waive it. The check is made out to the State of New Jersey, Division of Taxation, and goes with the paperwork to the settlement agent.

GIT/REP-4Seller with another exemptionWaiver requested from the Division before closing

Common GIT/REP exemptions and who signs

Whoever must sign the deed signs the form, whether that is the seller or an authorized representative holding a power of attorney or letter of authority. Each owner files. Married and civil union couples count as one owner, and an estate or trust files a single form that can carry several trustee or executor signatures.

  • The seller is a New Jersey resident.
  • Total consideration is $1,000 or less.
  • The seller is a business entity.
  • The seller is a nonresident claiming the principal residence exclusion.

Only sheriff's sales and bankruptcy trust sales skip the form. A county clerk can still reject a deed for reasons the Division does not control. If that happens, print the Division's GIT/REP instructions, highlight the passage that applies and show it to the clerk before you escalate.

Getting back an overpaid estimated payment

A nonresident seller can file Form A-3128 after closing to claim an early refund of an overpayment, with proof such as the settlement statement or closing disclosure. The form does not replace the NJ-1040-NR. That return is still due for the year the property sold, and the final refund comes out of it.

Since the 2 percent and 8.97 percent figures are only estimates, a seller with a small gain or a loss often overpays. Keep the closing disclosure, the deed and your improvement records together so the return is easy to prepare. A seller who expects a refund should file early, since nothing comes back until that return is processed.

Records to keep for the return

The gain is worked out on the tax return, not at the table, so keep the paperwork that proves your basis and the closing numbers. A nonresident who sold files the NJ-1040-NR for the year of the sale and lists the closing payment on the estimated payment line.

  • The settlement statement or closing disclosure from both the purchase and the sale.
  • Receipts for capital improvements. New Jersey does not allow certain federal deductions such as mortgage interest or capital improvements on the NJ-1040, so these receipts help with basis and not with a deduction.
  • The signed GIT/REP form and any payment receipt.
  • For an inherited house, papers showing its value when the owner died.

An estate's executor files one GIT/REP form for the sale. Ask the estate's tax preparer how the sale is reported on the estate's own return.

Frequently asked questions

Does New Jersey have its own capital gains tax on a home sale?

No separate tax exists. The state taxes the gain through its Gross Income Tax and follows the federal calculation, so a federally taxable amount is taxable here too.

What is the exclusion limit for spouses who sell together?

Spouses filing jointly can exclude up to $500,000 once the tests are met. When only one of them qualifies, the cap falls to $250,000.

Do I pay estimated tax at closing if I stay in New Jersey?

No. A resident who stays in the state submits form GIT/REP-3 and pays any income tax when filing the NJ-1040.

What if I sell and relocate out of New Jersey?

For this sale you count as a nonresident. The estimated payment applies unless an exemption fits, and a nonresident return follows for the year of the sale.

Which return reports the sale for a nonresident?

Form NJ-1040-NR, Part I, as Net Gains or Income From Disposition of Property, with any closing payment listed as an estimated payment.

What a sheriff sale is

A sheriff sale is the public auction that ends a New Jersey mortgage foreclosure. The Superior Court issues a writ of execution after final judgment, and that writ tells the county sheriff to sell the home to the highest bidder. New Jersey is a judicial foreclosure state, so every case runs through the Office of Foreclosure or a Superior Court General Equity judge.

Each county sheriff runs its own sales calendar, bidder rules and check-in routine. Morris County, Somerset County and Gloucester County all post their own terms, and the details differ from one county to the next. Ask the sheriff's sales unit in the county where the house sits for the current schedule before you plan around a date.

What has to happen before the sheriff can sell

The sheriff cannot list a home until the lender has finished several steps in court. The sequence runs like this:

  • The lender sends a Notice of Intent to Foreclose. The homeowner has 30 days from receipt to pay off the debt or reach another arrangement, and may ask for mediation.
  • The lender files a complaint, and the homeowner has 35 days to answer. No answer within 35 days makes the case uncontested.
  • Before asking for default, the lender gives a final chance to cure 14 days ahead. The homeowner then has 10 days to respond and 45 days to cure or work something out.
  • If the debt is not cured, the court enters final judgment and issues the writ of execution.

The notice of intent must also say that the homeowner can sell or transfer title. If you would rather sell the house than watch it go to auction, that line is your opening.

How long a sale can be delayed

The sheriff has 150 days from the writ of execution to auction the property. Inside that window the borrower and the lender may each ask for two stays, and a fifth is possible if both sides request it. In some cases a defendant can ask for one more stay to pursue mediation.

County rules add practical detail. Gloucester County gives each side two adjournments per foreclosure docket, with a written confirmation and a new sale date for the defendant. Morris County takes a Request for Statutory Adjournment form and requires it before noon on the scheduled sale day. A bankruptcy filing generally triggers an automatic stay, and the foreclosure resumes where it stopped once that case is resolved. The sheriff must also advertise the sale for at least four weeks before holding it.

How bidders buy at a sheriff sale

Bidding is an open outcry auction with no sealed bids, and the property goes to the highest bidder. The money terms match across the three counties. The winner pays at least 20 percent of the bid at the close of the sale, and the balance is due within 30 days. Interest runs on the balance from the 11th day after the sale, and extra time to arrange a mortgage is not granted.

Opening bids differ by county. In Somerset County the plaintiff opens at $1,000 and later bids rise in multiples of at least $1,000. Morris County and Gloucester County list a minimum bid of $100. Somerset no longer accepts cash for deposits or balances, Morris sets a $1,000 cash limit unless the sheriff approves more, and Gloucester requires a bidder registration form emailed by noon on the Tuesday before the sale.

  • A buyer gets a sheriff's deed once the full balance is paid, and the deed may not carry clear title.
  • Tax, sewer and water liens can follow the property, so the counties urge a title search before bidding.
  • Sales are subject to restrictions of record and to the rights of occupants or tenants.
  • No one may walk through the house beforehand, because the owner has no duty to allow an inspection.

Can the owner get the house back after the sale?

Yes, for a short time. The homeowner has 10 days after the auction to redeem, meaning to buy the property back or sell it. A successful redemption returns the bidder's deposit. Gloucester County adds that the 10 days can be extended only by a court order, and Somerset County notes that a bankruptcy filed in the same period puts the sale on hold until the court rules.

If nobody redeems, the sale proceeds first pay off the mortgage. Any amount left over returns to the homeowner. When the proceeds fall short, the lender can sue the homeowner for the remaining balance. If you suspect money is owed after the sale, ask the sheriff and the court clerk about surplus funds, and be careful with anyone who offers to chase that money for a fee.

What happens to the people living in the house

Occupants usually stay until some time after the auction. The lender's side must ask the court for a Writ of Possession, which instructs the sheriff to remove anyone still inside, and the sheriff tells the defendant the date to leave. A winning bidder has no right to enter until the deed is executed and a signed writ of possession is in hand.

Renters get separate protection. A residential tenant with a valid lease in good standing is not forced to move because of foreclosure, and the buyer at the sheriff sale takes the building subject to the tenant's rights. The anti-eviction statute, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12, is the law the court points to. A tenant served with a foreclosure complaint should speak to an attorney and can give the lender's lawyer a copy of the lease.

Paperwork and fees for a sheriff's deed

Two state forms show up in this process. When the sale is requested, a completed Affidavit of Consideration for Sheriff's Deeds, Form RTF-8, goes to the sheriff. It lists other mortgagees and the balance of prior mortgages and liens, and it is not an exemption from the Realty Transfer Fee. The second item is the gross income tax withholding form used for deed recording. Only sheriff's sales and bankruptcy trust sales are excused from signing the seller forms GIT/REP-1, -2 or -3.

The buyer records the deed with the county clerk and pays those recording fees. Court costs for the foreclosure itself are a lender matter, and they run $405 for a complaint, $175 for an answer or first appearance and $50 for a motion.

Options other than waiting for the sale

Options exist before and after judgment. A homeowner can reinstate the missed payments, pay the judgment, take a new loan, or sell. New Jersey offers free foreclosure mediation, and it is best to ask for it as early as possible after receiving the foreclosure notice. Where a case qualifies, the court also allows one extra stay of the sale for mediation.

Be wary of anyone promising a loan modification or foreclosure rescue, since these scams are spreading across New Jersey. A free HUD and NJHMFA certified housing counselor is a safer first call. Because the owner keeps the right to sell until the auction, a quick sale to a buyer who pays off the lender from proceeds can end the case without a sheriff's deed. A cash buyer skips the lender approval steps that slow an ordinary sale. Ask the lender's attorney for a written payoff figure before you set a closing date.

Frequently asked questions

How many days to redeem after a New Jersey sheriff sale?

Ten days. The 10 days start with the auction, and the owner can buy the house back or sell it in that window. County sheriffs say only a court order can extend the period.

Does a sheriff sale buyer have to pay all cash?

No. The winner pays at least 20 percent when the sale ends and the rest within 30 days, but counties do not grant extra time for a mortgage. Most sheriffs require certified funds, and some set a cash limit or ban cash.

Can a tenant be thrown out after a sheriff sale?

Not on the sale date alone. A tenant with a valid lease in good standing keeps tenant rights, and the buyer takes the building subject to them. Removal of an owner occupant needs a Writ of Possession.

Who gets the money left over from a sheriff sale?

The homeowner receives what remains after the mortgage debt is paid. If the proceeds do not cover the debt, the lender can sue for the difference.

How long does a sheriff have to sell after the writ of execution?

The sheriff has 150 days from the writ. Each side may request two stays and a fifth is possible if both agree, so the real timeline can run longer than the sale date first advertised.

How an eviction works from complaint to removal

A landlord files a landlord-tenant complaint in the Special Civil Part of the Superior Court, wins a judgment for possession, then asks the court for a warrant of removal that a court officer carries out. No one else can lawfully put a residential tenant out. Any other attempt is illegal.

The case is heard in the county courthouse where the rental sits. A landlord that is a corporation, LLC or limited partnership must be represented by a New Jersey attorney. A sole proprietor or general partnership may file without one, though a lawyer is a good idea.

The full sequence usually takes longer than the minimums suggest, since the tenant can ask for settlement time, a hardship stay or a later hearing. If you plan to sell an occupied rental, leave room for that.

Steps, fees and waiting periods

These are the court-set steps and the numbers that go with each.

Special Civil Part steps and timing
StepFee or waiting period
Filing the complaint$50 for one defendant, $5 for each added defendant, plus a $7 service fee
Trial dateAt least 21 days after the summons is served
Judgment for possessionTenant has three business days to pay rent and approved costs and stop the eviction
Warrant of removal$35 plus mileage; cannot issue until three business days after judgment

The officer's own eviction fee may not exceed $75. The landlord pays that and any second mileage fee directly.

What to file with the complaint

The packet is longer than many owners expect. The court's kit asks for the verified complaint, a tenancy summons, a Landlord Case Information Statement and a copy of the lease.

  • Lease provisions that treat fees and charges as additional rent, and any rental assistance notice or eviction-ground clauses.
  • A Registration Statement and a Certification of Lease and Registration Statement, unless the property is exempt under N.J.S.A. 46:8-27.
  • For any case other than unpaid rent, every notice sent to the tenant or housing authority that will be used at trial.

Registration depends on the owner. A landlord who lives on the property with three units or fewer registers with the municipal Community Development Authority, while other rentals register with the state Bureau of Housing Inspection. A missing registration can become a defense.

What happens at the trial date?

Both sides must show up. If the landlord does not appear, the case is dismissed. If the tenant does not appear, the court marks it a default and the landlord can apply for judgment.

When both appear, trained court staff first try to settle the matter. A settlement might give the tenant more time to move or set a payment plan, and a judge must review and approve it in residential cases where the tenant has no lawyer. With no deal, the judge hears the case and either grants or denies a judgment for possession.

The tenant cannot answer in writing. The defendant has to come in person, and witnesses must testify live because signed statements are not accepted.

How a tenant can stop or delay an eviction

Several tools exist, and each one can change a seller's timeline.

  • Pay in full: in a nonpayment case the tenant can pay all rent plus allowed costs before or at trial, or up to three business days after the eviction, and the landlord must accept it. A landlord who refuses or fails to tell the court faces a $500 penalty.
  • Orderly removal: an order giving up to seven more calendar days to move.
  • Hardship stay: up to six months, but only if the tenant pays everything owed and keeps paying rent during the stay.
  • Vacate the judgment: a request the court rarely grants.

Requests for orderly removal and a hardship stay must be made within 10 days of the eviction date. Payment from a charity or rental assistance program must also be accepted by the landlord.

Defenses a tenant can raise

New Jersey courts hear several common defenses, and any of them can stall a sale plan that assumes a quick removal.

  • Habitability: under the Marini Doctrine a tenant can withhold rent over problems like no heat or hot water, mold, rodents or a broken toilet, but only by depositing rent with the court and showing the landlord had a chance to fix it. It cannot excuse late payment patterns or noise violations.
  • Unregistered rental: no registration statement can sink the filing.
  • Illegal tenancy: a condemned property or an unapproved extra unit.
  • Abatement: the judge can reduce rent owed because of a defect.
  • Subsidy notice: a landlord must tell any public agency paying part of the rent, and the case can be dismissed if it did not.

Illegal lockouts

A lockout is any removal without a judgment for possession and a warrant carried out by a Special Civil Part officer. Changing the locks, padlocking the doors, and shutting off gas, water or electricity are all illegal ways to force a tenant out.

A landlord also cannot hold a tenant's furniture or belongings to force payment. A locked-out tenant can file in the Special Civil Part asking to be let back in and for damages.

Anyone buying a rented house should know this. A buyer who closes on an occupied property cannot clear it by self-help, and the same court process runs under the new owner's name. Back rent is a separate matter, since a judgment for possession does not award the unpaid amount and the landlord must sue for it in the special civil or small claims section.

Foreclosure and sheriff's sale

A tenant with a valid lease who is in good standing is generally not forced out because of foreclosure. Renters are pointed to the Anti-Eviction statute, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12, told to consult an attorney if served with a complaint, and told to give the lender's attorney a copy of the lease.

The purchaser at a sheriff's sale takes the building subject to tenants' rights. Tenants should also receive the court's Notice to Residential Tenants of Rights During Foreclosure.

The foreclosure process has a 30-day notice of intent, a 35-day window to answer a complaint, and a sheriff's sale that must happen within 150 days of the writ of execution. After the sale the debtor has 10 days to redeem. An owner with a tenant in the house and a mortgage in trouble can use that period to arrange a sale instead.

Options for selling a house with a tenant

There are three practical routes. Which one fits depends on the lease, the number of units and whether the tenant cooperates.

  • Sell with the tenant in place: the buyer takes over the tenancy, and the security deposit information must be updated in writing after a transfer.
  • Negotiate a move-out: a written agreement with the tenant, ideally reviewed by the court if a case is pending.
  • Use a recognized ground: a building of three units or fewer can be cleared for an owner or buyer who will live there, after two months' notice and once the lease ends.

After the tenant leaves, belongings left behind fall under New Jersey's abandoned property statute. Check with an attorney before you handle them.

Frequently asked questions

Can a New Jersey landlord change the locks to evict a tenant?

No. Changing locks, padlocking doors or cutting off utilities is an illegal lockout. Only a Special Civil Part officer can carry out an eviction, and only after a judgment for possession and a warrant of removal.

How long after a judgment does a tenant have to move out?

At least three business days after the warrant of removal is served. The warrant cannot issue until three business days after the judgment, so the minimum from judgment to eviction is about a week of business days.

Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying back rent?

Yes, in nonpayment cases. Paying all rent due plus approved costs before or on the hearing date, or within three business days after the eviction, leads to dismissal, and the landlord must accept cash, a cashier's check or a money order.

Does foreclosure automatically end a tenant's lease?

No. A tenant with a valid lease in good standing is not forced to move just because the property is in foreclosure, and the sheriff's sale buyer takes the building subject to the tenant's rights.

Do I need a lawyer to evict a tenant in New Jersey?

Only if the landlord is a corporation, LLC or limited partnership. Individual owners and sole proprietors can file on their own, but a lawyer is recommended if you can afford one.

What a quitclaim deed does

A quitclaim deed hands over whatever interest the signer holds, and it promises nothing about that interest. It conveys only the right, title or interest the grantor has or may have, with no warranty that the grantor owns any particular title.

New Jersey cares about the wording. For the deed to count as a true quitclaim, it must say so in specific language: that the deed is called a Quitclaim Deed, that the grantor makes no promises about ownership, and that the grantor simply transfers whatever interest exists. Nobody, lawyer or title agent, can imply it.

Because the deed carries no warranty, it suits transfers between people who already know the property's history, such as relatives or former co-owners, and it suits clearing up a possible claim on title. It is a poor fit when a buyer is paying market price and expects protection.

Is a quitclaim deed exempt from the transfer fee?

No. The label does not create an exemption. Attorneys often move freehold interests in quitclaim format, and those transfers are taxable for realty transfer fee purposes. Whether a deed escapes the fee depends on the relationship and the facts, not on the form name.

The county recording officer collects the fee when the deed is offered for recording, in addition to normal recording charges. Anyone claiming a full or partial exemption must file an Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller, Form RTF-1, which is notarized and recorded with the deed. Ask the county clerk or register of deeds for the current recording charges, because those are county fees and the state does not set them.

Family transfers and the exemption

The exemption most families look for covers deeds between husband and wife, or between parent and child. The state's own examples show how narrow it is.

Realty transfer fee treatment of common family deeds
Family transferFee treatment
Sale between parent and childExempt
Parent sells to daughter and her live-in boyfriendHalf of the price is exempt, half is taxable
Parent deeds to an adopted childFully exempt
Parent deeds to a stepchild who was not adoptedNot exempt
Parent places home in trust for the childrenNot exempt
Divorced spouse deeds a half interest under a settlement agreementNot exempt
Estate sale to a buyer not named in the willNot exempt

The divorce answer turns on a detail. A settlement agreement that is merely folded into a divorce judgment keeps its consensual character, so the exemption for a transfer made under a final judgment applies only when a judge orders the transfer.

Forms that go with a New Jersey deed

A deed cannot be recorded without a Gross Income Tax form. N.J.S.A. 54A:8-9 requires a GIT/REP form for a transfer of real property, and it is submitted at closing along with the RTF-1. The Division of Taxation uses the forms to find out whether a nonresident seller must prepay estimated gross income tax on the transfer.

Family deeds get no special treatment here. There is no parent-to-child exemption for the GIT/REP requirements, so the seller's residency, whether the home is a principal residence, the consideration and any net proceeds are looked at the same way as in any other sale. For a nonresident who quitclaims property to a sibling or ex-spouse for $1,000 or less, the GIT/REP-3 is used, with the box for consideration of $1,000 or less checked.

Consideration includes open mortgages, so a deed that looks like a gift can still carry a taxable amount when a loan stays on the property. The forms to expect with a family deed are:

  • Form RTF-1, the notarized affidavit of consideration, recorded with the deed
  • a GIT/REP form chosen by the seller's residency and the price
  • Form RTF-3, only if a refund is needed after a wrong-county filing

The 1 percent fee on larger transfers

A 1 percent fee applies to the buyer when the total consideration is more than $1,000,000. People call it the mansion tax. Buying spouses cannot dodge it by signing separate contracts and receiving separate deeds, because the intent to buy one property together makes the combined price the consideration.

The fee is not imposed when the buyer is an organization the IRS has determined to be exempt from federal income tax, or when the transfer meets New Jersey's exempt transaction rules. Most family quitclaim deeds fall far below the threshold, so this fee matters mainly for high-value property.

Where to record, and what if the county is wrong?

Filing happens at the recording office for the county that contains the parcel. After closing, the title agent or attorney usually files it. If a deed is recorded in the wrong county, record it again where the land actually sits, then file Form RTF-3 for a refund of the State portion and ask the wrong county's recording office for a refund of the county portion.

That mistake costs fees and time, so confirm the county before signing.

Other deeds the fee skips

A few transactions that look like deeds are treated differently. A lease of less than 99 years is not a deed for these purposes, unless the lease or contract lets either side extend it beyond 99 years, in which case the transfer is taxable. A corporation or LLC that only changes its name can record a confirmatory deed with no fee once it gives the county recording officer and the fee unit a copy of the state certificate of amendment. A transfer incidental to a corporate merger may avoid the 1 percent fee when the real property is under 20 percent of the value of everything exchanged, but the grantee must file the stamped merger document with Form RTF-4.

When a quitclaim deed makes sense before a sale

A quitclaim deed fits a limited set of situations in New Jersey, and it is not a shortcut around the tax rules.

  • adding or removing a relative from title when the exempt relationships above apply
  • releasing an ex-spouse's or co-heir's interest as part of an agreed buyout, with the fee calculated on the price plus the right share of any mortgage
  • confirming a name change on an entity's existing deed, which can be recorded without a transfer fee once the state certificate is on file
  • settling a possible claim on title before a buyer's title company reviews it

When the goal is a sale to an outside buyer, a deed with warranties is normally what the buyer's lender and title agent expect. Talk with a New Jersey attorney or title agent before choosing the deed type. If you plan to sell, ask the title agent early which forms your closing will need, so the notarized affidavit and the GIT/REP form are ready before the deed goes to the recording office.

Frequently asked questions

Does a quitclaim deed remove my mortgage?

No. A quitclaim deed changes who holds the ownership interest, not what is owed on the loan. Open mortgage balances count as consideration for fee purposes, so an unpaid mortgage can raise the realty transfer fee on a family deed.

Do I pay a transfer fee when I add my child to a deed?

Often not, because a sale or deed between parent and child is an exempt transaction. A stepchild who was not adopted is not covered, and a transfer into a trust for the children is taxable.

Where do I record a quitclaim deed in New Jersey?

File it with the recording office of the county that contains the parcel. After a filing in the wrong county, record again in the right one and apply for refunds using Form RTF-3 and the wrong county's refund process.

Is a quitclaim deed the same as a warranty deed?

No. A quitclaim passes only the interest the grantor has and makes no promise about title. New Jersey also requires specific wording for a deed to qualify as a true quitclaim.

Can a nonresident quitclaim a New Jersey property?

Yes, but a GIT/REP form is still needed to record the deed. A nonresident who conveys by quitclaim for $1,000 or less completes the GIT/REP-3 and checks the box for consideration of $1,000 or less.

What gets sold at a tax sale

A bidder buys a lien certificate, and the owner keeps the deed. Title to a delinquent property is not auctioned. The certificate is a claim against the property for the unpaid tax, and it stays there until the owner redeems it or a Superior Court judgment ends the right to redeem.

A municipality that has delinquent property taxes or other municipal charges must hold at least one tax sale a year. Each town runs its own calendar, so call the municipal tax collector in the town where the house sits to learn when the next sale is set.

The lien builds up through four installment dates: February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. An unpaid balance can draw interest of up to 8 percent on the first $1,500 and up to 18 percent on anything above that. When the delinquency passes $10,000 at the end of the municipal fiscal year, the town may add a penalty of up to 6 percent.

How bidding works, and who holds the extra money

Bidders compete to take the lowest interest rate, and the winner is the one who accepts the least. The auction starts at the top rate allowed and bids go down. If bidding reaches the floor of one percent, bidders then offer a cash premium, starting at zero, and the highest premium wins.

The premium does not pay down your taxes. The municipality keeps it on deposit, and under R.S. 54:5-33 as amended in 2024 it goes back to the certificate holder when the owner redeems. If nobody redeems or forecloses within five years of the sale, the premium becomes municipal money.

  • The winning bidder pays the town the back taxes and interest at the close of the sale.
  • The holder should record the certificate in the county clerk's deed room within 90 days.
  • Taxes keep accruing after the sale, and a holder may pay them and earn the rate the municipality sets.
  • A later certificate on the same house ranks ahead of the earlier one.

How long before a holder can start a foreclosure?

A town that bought its own certificate can sue after six months. Anyone else who holds a certificate must wait two years from the sale date. Once a suit is filed, the right to redeem continues until the court's judgment bars it.

An abandoned property follows a faster path. A holder of a certificate on a property that meets the state's abandoned property definition may file at any time, with a certification from the public officer or tax collector, or with sworn professional evidence if that certification was refused.

What it costs to redeem

The cost is the tax, the certificate interest, and a redemption penalty of 2, 4 or 6 percent that depends on the size of the certificate. Fees stack on top once a private holder starts the legal process, so the figure grows the longer the lien sits.

A private holder who wants search and counsel fees must first mail the owner a written notice by certified mail at least 30 days before filing the complaint. That notice has to state the redemption amount and tell the owner about the right to ask for a judicial sale. Before the complaint is filed, the holder may add only a few items:

  • A title or foreclosure search fee of no more than $350.
  • Reasonable attorney fees of no more than $150.
  • Postage and certified mailing costs for the notice.
  • A calculation fee the town charges, which an ordinance may cap at $50.

After the complaint is on file, the attorney fee is set at $2,500 plus listed expenses such as court filing fees, service of process, a title search up to $350, publication and sheriff's fees. Redemption then happens only inside that court case, and the court may direct payment to the tax collector at the municipal office.

Keeping the equity if a certificate is foreclosed

You can, but only by asking in writing before the final judgment. Under P.L. 2024, c.39, the owner or the owner's heirs may send the Superior Court a written demand that the property go to a judicial sale or a sheriff's internet auction instead of passing straight to the certificate holder.

The amount the sale brings is treated as the property's market value. If nobody bids, the law presumes there was no equity. The sheriff deposits any surplus with the clerk of the Superior Court, and the owner claims it by motion. If the owner made the demand, the certificate holder gets a first lien on 10 percent of the surplus, capped at $5,000, for administrative costs.

Without a timely demand, the holder can foreclose with no sale, and the owner has no claim for any equity. The summons, complaint and published notice must show this right in bold type. The abandoned property route is the exception, because that suit does not require a judicial sale.

How a city like Newark runs its sales

Newark runs two kinds. A standard tax sale covers prior years' taxes and municipal charges that remain unpaid in the current year. An accelerated tax sale covers the current year's charges that are still owed after the statutory due date of November 10. Either way, the city sells a lien certificate and the property can face foreclosure if it is not redeemed in time.

A partial payment goes to the oldest quarter first. An owner who is behind on three quarters and pays something in September sees that money applied to the first quarter's principal and interest. Owners who want a payoff figure can call the tax customer service lines on weekdays.

Can selling the house solve the problem?

Often it can, because the lien is paid from the sale price at closing and the buyer receives clear title. The earlier the sale closes, the smaller the payoff, since interest, the redemption penalty and foreclosure fees all grow with time.

  • Ask the tax collector for a written redemption figure good through the expected closing date.
  • If a foreclosure complaint has been filed, expect the $2,500 attorney fee and court costs to be inside that figure.
  • Send the written demand for a judicial sale before final judgment if you want any equity protected and the sale to your own buyer cannot close first.
  • Tell your closing attorney or title company about any recorded certificate so it is paid and discharged at the table.

A deed given on a sale for delinquent taxes is among the deeds exempt from the realty transfer fee. An ordinary sale by the owner is not exempt, so budget for that fee on the closing statement.

Frequently asked questions

Can I lose my house over a small unpaid tax bill?

Yes, the certificate can be foreclosed after the waiting period, which is six months for a town holder and two years for other holders. Until a judgment is entered, you can still redeem by paying the tax, interest, penalty and any allowed fees. A written demand for a judicial sale or sheriff's internet auction before final judgment protects the equity.

Who receives the premium that a bidder pays?

The municipality holds it. It goes back to the certificate holder if the owner redeems and moves into the town's funds if nobody redeems or forecloses within five years. The owner's taxes are not reduced by it.

What can a private holder add to my bill before suing?

Only a title or foreclosure search fee up to $350, attorney fees up to $150, postage and certified mailing costs, and any calculation fee the town charges. The holder must send a 30-day certified mail notice first, and the notice must state the redemption amount.

Do I have to move out after a tax sale?

No. The sale transfers a lien certificate and the owner keeps title and possession. Only a final court judgment that bars redemption changes who holds the deed.

Who do I call to find the payoff?

Call the tax collector in the municipality where the house sits and ask for a redemption figure dated to your closing day. Ask whether the certificate belongs to the town or to a private holder, because that decides the foreclosure timeline and who receives payment.

How a property tax lien starts

In New Jersey, property taxes are a continuous lien on the real estate from the moment they are due. There are four installment dates: February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. Unpaid amounts accrue interest, and the rate may reach 8 percent on the first $1,500 of delinquency and 18 percent on anything above that.

A year-end penalty of up to 6 percent can be added when a delinquency tops $10,000 at the close of the municipal fiscal year. Rates and fees can change, so ask the municipal tax collector which figures apply to your bill. The tax collector, not the county, runs the process for a house in your town.

What is sold at a tax sale?

The deed stays with the owner, and the buyer purchases a tax sale certificate, which is a lien on the property. All 566 municipalities must hold at least one tax sale a year if they have delinquent taxes or other municipal charges. The list of properties has to be prepared at least 50 days before the sale, and the notice is posted in public places and published as a legal ad.

Bidding runs downward. Opening bids start at the maximum 18 percent rate, with bidders dropping the rate toward zero. At zero the bidding turns to a dollar premium, so the winner is the lowest rate or, at zero, the highest premium. When nobody bids, the municipality takes the certificate at 18 percent. The premium stays on deposit with the town for up to five years under R.S. 54:5-33 as amended in 2024, and it passes to the municipality if the lien is not redeemed or foreclosed in that time.

What stops a property from going to tax sale

Paying before the sale date stops it. A payment goes first to interest, costs and penalties, and then to the oldest delinquent principal. Close to the sale date the office may require a bank check, because personal checks are not accepted, so call the collection office before sending money. A notice stamped "Subject to Tax Sale" on a bill means last year's unpaid amount is on the list, although the current year's balance may be unpaid too.

Other towns set their own sale dates. Look for the notice on your town's website or call the tax office.

Who can redeem a certificate?

Only a short list of people can redeem: the owner, the owner's heirs, a holder of a prior outstanding certificate, a mortgagee and a legal occupant of the property. They may redeem only until the right to redeem is cut off. Payment goes to the tax collector in full, by cash or certified funds.

  • The amount due is the certificate plus interest and any later taxes the lien holder paid.
  • Each later payment by the investor adds to what the owner owes, which is why the balance grows.
  • After redeeming, the owner receives the cancelled certificate and is responsible for having the lien removed at the county office.

If you are selling a house with a certificate on it, ask the tax collector for a payoff good through the closing date, then confirm the cancellation is recorded after closing.

What redemption costs beyond the unpaid tax

The certificate holder earns money while the lien sits. A certificate redeemed before foreclosure earns a redemption penalty of 2, 4 or 6 percent, depending on the size of the original certificate, on top of the interest rate bid at the sale. Taxes keep accruing after the sale as well. The investor may pay them, and if nobody does, a later certificate is sold at the next tax sale and ranks ahead of the earlier one.

Investors are told to record the certificate with the County Clerk within 90 days of the sale. That recording is what shows up in a title search, so a house with a certificate on it will usually be flagged before a buyer closes. The 2024 law also lets a certificate holder on an abandoned property enter after certified-mail notice to make repairs or remove hazards, and those costs can be added to the unpaid balance.

When the lien holder can foreclose

A municipality that holds the certificate may sue to foreclose the right of redemption once six months have gone by from the date of sale. Any other holder must wait two years, under R.S. 54:5-86 as amended by P.L. 2024, c.39. Abandoned property is the exception, and a holder may file at any time. Until the Superior Court enters judgment, the right to redeem continues.

Earliest foreclosure suit by type of holder
Certificate holderEarliest foreclosure suit

Investor or other buyer2 years after the sale
Any holder, abandoned propertyAny time
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Jersey houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What P.L. 2024, c.39 changed for owners

The law was approved July 10, 2024 and covers any lien not yet foreclosed on that date. Its biggest change protects equity. In a foreclosure on a tax sale certificate, the owner or heirs may demand in writing, before final judgment, that the holder go through a judicial sale or a sheriff's internet auction, the way a mortgage is foreclosed. If no demand is made, the holder can foreclose without a sale and the owner has no claim for equity.

  • The summons and complaint must carry a bold notice of this right.
  • The sheriff pays surplus funds to the Superior Court clerk, and the owner applies for them by motion.
  • A holder that is not a municipality must give 30 days' written notice by certified mail before filing, or it cannot recover search and counsel fees.
  • Once a foreclosure complaint is filed, attorney's fees of $2,500 are added to the redemption amount, plus listed costs and a title search fee capped at $350.
  • If the owner asked for a sale, the holder takes a first lien of 10 percent of the surplus for administrative costs, up to $5,000.

Handling a tax lien when selling the house

Start by asking the tax collector which certificates exist and which charges remain unpaid. A buyer will expect clear title, and a redemption that includes foreclosure costs is more expensive than one made early. If a complaint has been filed, redemption must be made in that case, and the court can set attorney's fees and costs at any point.

A sale also gives you a way to protect equity. If you sell for market value and pay the redemption amount from proceeds, you keep the remainder. Waiting through a foreclosure without demanding a sale can mean losing that equity.

Gather the certificate details, the payoff letter and any notices you have received before you talk with a buyer or title company. A cash sale can close on a date you pick, which helps when a foreclosure clock is running. Legal Services of New Jersey runs a statewide hotline at 1-888-LSNJ-LAW for owners who cannot afford a lawyer.

Frequently asked questions

What is a tax sale certificate in New Jersey?

It is a lien sold at auction for unpaid taxes or municipal charges. The buyer does not receive the deed, but may earn interest and can foreclose if the owner never redeems.

How long do owners have to redeem before foreclosure?

Two years when an investor holds the certificate, and six months when the municipality does. Redemption stays open until the Superior Court enters a final judgment barring it.

Can an owner lose a house over a small tax debt?

Yes, if the certificate goes unredeemed and the holder completes a foreclosure. The 2024 law lets the owner demand a judicial sale or sheriff internet auction before final judgment to preserve equity.

Do fees get added to a tax lien in New Jersey?

Yes. After a foreclosure complaint, the redemption amount includes $2,500 in attorney's fees and listed costs, with a search fee capped at $350. Earlier notice costs are smaller.

Who do I call to get a redemption figure?

Call the municipal tax collector in the town where the house sits. Ask for a written payoff good through your planned closing date.

What a New Jersey seller pays at closing

Expect one state fee, one possible state surcharge and a handful of private costs. The Realty Transfer Fee falls on the seller at recording, and the buyer owes none of it. No sales tax applies to a home sale. Your sale contract and your lender decide the private costs, and those change with every deal.

  • The Realty Transfer Fee, a rate applied to the price shown in the deed.
  • A graduated percent fee when the price tops $1,000,000.
  • Broker compensation, whatever your written agreement says.
  • An estimated income tax deposit if you live outside New Jersey and no exemption fits.
  • The mortgage payoff and any property tax still owed.

Most sellers also supply form RTF-1, the Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller. A deed that claims any exemption must carry that affidavit.

How the Realty Transfer Fee is calculated

The fee is stacked in slices: a dollar amount for each $500, at a higher rate for each higher slice of the price. It starts from the price stated in the deed. In a few situations the Division of Taxation substitutes assessed value divided by the Director's Ratio. Every deed that conveys title is covered unless an exemption fits.

Fee schedule for a standard sale priced above $350,000
Slice of the priceRate per $500
$0 to $150,000$2.90
$150,000 to $200,000$4.25
$200,000 to $550,000$4.80
$550,000 to $850,000$5.30
$850,000 to $1,000,000$5.80
Above $1,000,000$6.05

A cheaper schedule governs any sale at $350,000 or below, starting at $2.00 per $500 and topping out at $3.90. Qualifying seniors, blind or disabled persons and low and moderate income housing use reduced rates. The senior and disability reduction belongs to the person, so an estate or trust cannot claim it.

To see your own number, add up each slice of your price at its rate. Your closing attorney or title agent will run the exact figure, and you should ask for it before you set a net price.

The percent fee on sales above $1 million

This is a percentage of the full sale price, owed once consideration passes $1,000,000. Since P.L. 2025, c. 69 took effect on July 10, 2025, the seller pays it instead of the buyer. Older write-ups that call it a 1 percent buyer's mansion tax no longer describe deeds submitted on or after that date.

  • 1% of total consideration when the price runs from $1,000,000 up to $2,000,000.
  • 2% above $2,000,000 up to $2,500,000.
  • 2.5% above $2,500,000 up to $3,000,000.
  • 3% above $3,000,000 up to $3,500,000.
  • 3.5% on prices above $3,500,000.

Each rate applies to the entire price, so the cost jumps at every threshold instead of building slice by slice. A seller close to $2,000,000 or $2,500,000 should get the exact figure from the closing attorney before accepting an offer. The fee covers Class 2 residential property, farms with a residential building, Class 4A commercial property and cooperative units.
