Deeds that escape the transfer fee

The Division lists a long set of full exemptions, and the seller claims one on form RTF-1. Check the facts closely, because each exemption is read narrowly.

  • Husband and wife, or parent and child, with adopted children counted and stepchildren left out.
  • An executor or administrator passing the house to a named devisee or legal heir.
  • Deeds for consideration under $100.
  • A deed whose only job is to confirm or fix one already on record.
  • Tax sale deeds and deeds on partition.
  • A deed between divorced spouses filed within 90 days after the decree.

Some transfers look exempt and are not. An executor who sells to someone not named in the will pays the fee. A will that orders a sale and a split of the cash is treated as a gift of money. Moving a house into a trust for other beneficiaries is taxable, and the terms of a divorce settlement agreement do not count as specific performance of a judgment. At a sheriff's sale, form RTF-8 is also required, and it is not an exemption.

Who sets broker compensation in New Jersey?

You and your brokerage do, in writing. Under P.L. 2024, c. 32, effective August 1, 2024, the brokerage must sign a brokerage services agreement with the seller in every residential transaction. It states the term, the amount of compensation and how it is calculated, and it must say that compensation is fully negotiable and not set by law (DOBI Bulletin 24-11).

  • Compensation can be a flat fee, a percentage of the price or another lawful method.
  • It can be paid by the seller, the buyer, a third party, or shared between brokerages.
  • The agreement must show whether the agency is exclusive or non-exclusive.
  • The brokerage must obtain a signed property condition disclosure statement from the seller.

Showings changed too. At a residential showing open to the public, agents must post a sign saying the agent represents the seller and that what a visitor tells the agent is not confidential. Read the agency section before you sign. New Jersey law recognizes seller's agents, buyer's agents, disclosed dual agents, designated agents and transaction brokers, and each owes you different duties.

Where the deed is recorded

The clerk of the county that contains the parcel records the deed. The package includes the RTF paperwork and a GIT/REP form, two separate requirements handed in at closing. Whether to accept the package is the clerk's decision.

If the package went to the wrong county, record it again in the right one. Form RTF-3 recovers the state share, and the county share needs a separate request to the office that took it by mistake. Have your title agent confirm the county before anything is mailed.

Getting ready for closing

A little preparation keeps the closing day quiet. Ask the closing attorney or title agent for a written list of what comes out of your proceeds, and compare it to the items above: the Realty Transfer Fee, any percent fee, broker compensation, the mortgage payoff and unpaid property tax.

  • Bring your signed brokerage services agreement and the property condition disclosure statement.
  • Have the RTF-1 ready if any exemption is claimed on the deed.
  • Complete the right GIT/REP form. A seller living outside New Jersey also faces the estimated tax deposit, which is credited on the later tax return.
  • Ask for the mortgage payoff figure as of the closing date.

Selling to a cash buyer who takes the house as is removes lender appraisal and repair negotiations from the picture, but the state fees above still apply to the deed, so ask any buyer to confirm in writing which closing costs they expect you to cover.

Frequently asked questions

Which side of the table owes the transfer fee?

The seller does. It is collected at recording, and a buyer on an ordinary purchase owes none of it.

Does a house sale carry sales tax?

No. Home sales are outside sales tax in New Jersey.

What does the fee run on a $325,000 sale?

It runs $1,910 with no exemption, using the cheaper schedule for prices of $350,000 or below.

Does the old mansion tax still fall on buyers?

For deeds submitted on or after July 10, 2025, the seller owes the graduated percent fee on prices above $1,000,000. The rate starts at 1 percent and climbs to 3.5 percent.

Can I negotiate the real estate commission?

Yes. Broker compensation is fully negotiable, not set by law, and must appear in the brokerage services agreement.

Who handles probate in New Jersey?

Each of New Jersey's 21 counties has a Surrogate's Court, and the surrogate of the county where the person lived handles the estate paperwork. The state judiciary publishes a directory with the street address and phone number of every office, from Atlantic and Bergen through Union and Warren.

The person who runs the estate is the executor named in a will or, when there is no will, an administrator. That representative files the inheritance tax return and asks for the waivers that release bank accounts and real estate. If you inherit a house in New Jersey, call the surrogate's office first. Staff can tell you which papers a will needs, which an intestate estate needs, and what the fees are.

Can a small estate skip formal administration?

Sometimes, but the dollar limits are low and they include real estate. Under N.J.S.A. 3B:10-3, as amended by P.L. 2015, c. 232, a surviving spouse, civil union partner or domestic partner can take an intestate estate without administration when total real and personal assets do not exceed $50,000. The survivor signs an affidavit before the county surrogate, and the first $10,000 of the estate is free from the decedent's debts.

With no surviving spouse or partner, N.J.S.A. 3B:10-4 lets one heir collect the assets of an intestate estate worth no more than $20,000, after getting the written consent of the other heirs and signing an affidavit with the surrogate. Both rules count real property. A house in most New Jersey towns is worth far more than these limits, so a home sale almost always goes through a full appointment as executor or administrator.

Inheritance tax and an inherited house

New Jersey charges a transfer inheritance tax that depends on who receives the property, and it can hold up a sale. New Jersey financial and real estate assets in the decedent's name stay frozen until any inheritance tax is assessed and paid. The return and payment are due within eight months of the date of death.

Beneficiaries fall into four classes, and the class sets the rate:

New Jersey inheritance tax classes
ClassWho is includedTax
ASpouse, civil union or domestic partner, children, grandchildren, parents, grandparents, stepchildrenExempt
CSiblings, sons-in-law and daughters-in-law11% to 16% after a $25,000 exemption per beneficiary
DNieces, nephews, cousins, friends, ex-spouses, uncertified partners15% on the first $700,000, then 16%
ECharitable institutionsExempt

A full return is required whenever anything passes to a Class C, D or E beneficiary, a mutually acknowledged child or a trust. Unpaid tax draws 10 percent annual interest, and asking for more time to file does not move the payment date.

Getting permission to transfer or sell the property

Real estate cannot move out of the decedent's name without a tax waiver from the state. Form 0-1 is issued only by the Division of Taxation, it is not available for download, and real estate transfers always require it. When every beneficiary is exempt and no tax is owed, the executor files a Form L-9 affidavit with the Inheritance and Estate Tax Branch to receive the 0-1 for real estate.

A few related points:

  • Form L-8, a self-executing waiver, works for bank accounts only when no inheritance or estate tax is due and nothing is filed with the state
  • banks may release up to 50 percent of the funds on hand to the executor, administrator or a joint owner before a waiver arrives
  • property that a spouse or civil union partner holds as tenants by the entirety, and passes to the survivor, needs no waiver and is not reported
  • assets should be reported at their fair market value on the date of death, not on the filing date

Allow time. Plan for several months of processing after a return is filed, and about 40 to 50 percent of returns are audited, which adds more months. The Inheritance and Estate Tax Hotline is 609-292-5033, open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Does New Jersey still have an estate tax?

Not for recent deaths. Whether an estate tax return was needed depended on the year of death: the exemption was $675,000 for 2016 and earlier, $2 million for 2017, and for deaths in 2018 or after every estate is exempt and no return is needed. The inheritance tax is a separate tax and still applies to Class C and D beneficiaries.

An estate never pays more than the higher of the two state taxes, so executors check both. Federal estate tax is a different matter and is not handled by the state branch.

Is the sale of an inherited house exempt from the realty transfer fee?

It depends on who the buyer is. A transfer by an executor to the devisees or heirs named in the will or the intestacy law is exempt. A sale by the executor to anyone else is not. A will that directs the house to be sold and the money divided among children does not change this, because bequests of sale money are treated as gifts of money rather than devises of land.

The senior, blind or disabled partial exemption is personal and cannot be given to a decedent or an estate. A sale to an outside buyer therefore carries the fee. Ask the county clerk or the title agent for the fee figure before you set a net price.

Steps that help an heir sell during probate

The order of tasks matters more than the speed of any one task. A New Jersey heir can keep the sale moving by doing these things early:

  • obtain the death certificate and the original will, and ask the county surrogate how to qualify as executor or administrator
  • list every beneficiary and work out its tax class to learn whether a full return is required
  • file the L-9 or the IT-R, depending on the class, and request the Form 0-1 for the house
  • keep property taxes, insurance and utilities current while the waiver is pending
  • choose a buyer who can close once the waiver issues and the representative holds court-issued authority

A buyer who pays cash and accepts the house as is can shorten the repair and financing steps, but the waiver and the surrogate's appointment still control the closing date.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need probate to sell a house I inherited in New Jersey?

In most cases yes. A house usually exceeds the $50,000 and $20,000 small-estate limits, and real estate transfers always need a Form 0-1 waiver from the Division of Taxation. A surviving spouse who holds the home as tenants by the entirety is the main exception.

How long do I have to file the inheritance tax return?

Eight months from the date of death. When that date does not exist in the later month, the due date is the first day of the following month. Unpaid tax carries 10 percent annual interest.

Do children pay inheritance tax on a parent's house?

No. Children, grandchildren, parents and spouses are Class A beneficiaries and are exempt. Siblings are Class C and pay 11 percent to 16 percent after a $25,000 exemption, while nieces, nephews and friends are Class D at 15 percent to 16 percent.

Can a bank release money before the waiver arrives?

Partly. Banks may release up to 50 percent of the funds on hand to the executor, administrator or a joint account owner before a waiver is received. They must also pay checks written to New Jersey Inheritance and Estate Tax from the account.

Is there a New Jersey estate tax on a recent death?

No. For deaths in 2018 or after, all estates are exempt and no estate tax return is required. Inheritance tax may still apply to Class C and D beneficiaries.

What a New Jersey seller must disclose

A New Jersey seller of a home must complete a property condition disclosure statement, known as the PCDS, and sign it. The form comes from the Division of Consumer Affairs under N.J.A.C. 13:45A-29.1(d), and the statute behind it is N.J.S.A. 56:8-19.1. P.L. 2024, c.32 made it a duty for real estate brokerage firms to obtain the signed statement from a residential seller.

A seller without an agent has the same job. A seller who is not working with a brokerage firm, or who works with a firm acting as transaction broker, must hand the statement to the buyer before the buyer becomes obligated under any contract. Timing matters here. A statement delivered after the contract is signed does not meet the rule as written in section 2(e) of P.L. 2024, c.32.

Flood disclosure

Since March 20, 2024, every seller of real property in the state must disclose flood risk information through the PCDS before the buyer is bound by a purchase contract. There are two parts. You state whether the property is in FEMA's Special Flood Hazard Area or Moderate Flood Hazard Area, and you report any actual knowledge about the property's flood risks.

The law is P.L. 2023, c.94, enacted July 3, 2023. The Department of Environmental Protection offers a Flood Risk Notification Tool to help sellers find the zone answers. The duty applies to every seller, so a cash sale or an as-is sale does not remove the question.

Other disclosures when you sell a house

The Department of Banking and Insurance publishes a consumer guide that lists the items beyond the statement. Several belong to the seller, and others are mostly for the buyer to investigate.

  • Lead paint: for a house built before 1978, the seller must disclose known lead-based paint and hazards, give the buyer a lead disclosure form, and share any records or reports.
  • Material physical conditions: P.L. 2024, c.32 requires the listing brokerage to disclose existing material information about the property's physical condition that it knows or that a reasonable effort would reveal.
  • Stigmatized property: a seller and agent do not have to volunteer a haunting or a violent death, but must answer truthfully if the buyer asks.
  • Off-site conditions: municipal clerks keep lists of nearby conditions that may affect value, and buyers can review them.
  • Megan's Law: the county prosecutor decides how notice is given about convicted offenders in an area.

Mold, radon and asbestos are inspection topics for the buyer, so expect questions about them during an inspection even though they are not separate seller forms.

What changed under P.L. 2024, c.32

The law was signed July 10, 2024 and became effective August 1, 2024. It adds designated agency as a fifth business relationship and requires a written brokerage services agreement in residential deals. Compensation terms in that agreement must say expressly that broker pay is negotiable and not set by law.

The Act also requires a posted sign at residential open houses warning visitors that the agent represents the seller and that information given to the agent is not confidential. If you list with an agent, expect to sign the agency disclosure at the start and to hand over the PCDS soon after.

Seller paperwork and when each piece applies
PaperworkWhen it applies
Signed PCDS to agent or buyerBefore the buyer is obligated by a contract
Flood risk answersEvery seller, since March 20, 2024
Lead paint formHouses built before 1978
Brokerage services agreementResidential transactions, from August 1, 2024

Can a buyer or seller walk away after signing?

An attorney review clause gives both sides a window. When a licensee prepares the contract of sale, it must give buyer and seller three business days from delivery of the fully signed contract to consult an attorney. In that period the attorney can propose revisions or cancel the contract. If you hired an attorney to draft the contract instead, the review period may or may not be included, so ask the attorney.

This is where disclosure answers get tested. A statement that mentions flooding, a past repair or a lead history can lead the buyer's lawyer to ask for a repair credit or a price change during the review days. Answering fully at the start keeps those three days from turning into a renegotiation of surprises.

After the buyer's inspection

An independent home inspection is recommended soon after a contract becomes binding, with the buyer present. The inspector reports on the structure, construction and mechanical systems and flags defects or items to replace. If the report shows problems, buyer and seller are held to the time limits written in the contract for delivering the report and for the seller to decide whether to correct the items.

Read those inspection and response deadlines before you sign. Missing the contract's response window can leave you without a say in how a repair issue gets resolved. Ask your agent or attorney about the specifics of your contract.

Seller taxes and forms at closing

The seller pays the Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded. It is calculated from the consideration in the deed, using a rate per $500 that rises with price. For a deal of $350,000 or less, the rate is $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 from $200,000 to $350,000. An Affidavit of Consideration, Form RTF-1, claims any exemption. Sales above $1,000,000 also carry a graduated percent fee that starts at 1 percent of consideration.

A GIT/REP form is also recorded with the deed. New Jersey resident individuals, estates and trusts sign the GIT/REP-3. A nonresident seller prepays estimated gross income tax unless an assurance on that form applies, and the payment cannot be less than 2 percent of the total consideration in the deed. Executors and trustees complete the form for the estate or trust.

Selling while in foreclosure

You can still sell. The Notice of Intent to Foreclose must state that the debtor can sell or transfer the title. After a sheriff sale the owner also has 10 days to redeem by buying back or selling. Disclosure rules still apply to a distressed sale, so the PCDS, flood answers and any lead form go to the buyer the same way.

Watch out for foreclosure rescue and loan modification scams, and consider a free HUD and NJHMFA certified housing counselor. Anyone who asks for an upfront fee to save a home deserves a second look before you sign. A seller with a foreclosure on the calendar should ask the lender's attorney for a payoff figure, so the buyer's closing date and the lender's schedule can be matched.

Frequently asked questions

Is the disclosure statement required for every New Jersey home sale?

For residential sales, yes. A licensee must obtain the signed statement from the seller, and a seller without an agent must give it to the buyer before the buyer is bound by the contract.

Do I have to disclose that my house floods?

Yes, to the extent you know. Every seller must state whether the property is in a FEMA Special or Moderate Flood Hazard Area and report actual knowledge of flood risk before the buyer is obligated.

Is lead paint disclosure required in New Jersey?

Yes for houses built before 1978. The seller discloses known lead-based paint and hazards, provides the lead disclosure form and passes along any records or reports in hand.

Must a seller disclose a death in the house?

Not unless asked. Stigmatized property, such as a violent death, does not have to be volunteered, but a seller or agent who knows the answer must give it truthfully when a buyer asks.

Who pays the realty transfer fee in New Jersey?

The seller pays it. Rates are set per $500 of consideration, and the fee is collected when the deed is recorded with the county clerk.
